# Draft:Cryptocurrency Regulation in the United Kingdom__disambig_1

CRYPTOCURRENCY REGULATION IN THE UNITED KINGDOM
INTRODUCTION
In the UK, cryptocurrency regulation is defined as the policies crafted by the Government, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), and other relevant bodies concerning digital currencies and the services linked to them.
In April 2022, the UK government announced plans to position the country as a global hub for innovation in crypto assets, while asserting that they would retain high regulatory benchmarks. This has resulted in the UK government actively attempting to strike a balance between fostering innovation and protecting consumers and financial stability.
HISTORY OF CRYPTOCURRENCY REGULATION IN THE UNITED KINGDOM
In the UK, the first few years saw little to no oversight concerning the regulation of cryptocurrencies. During the years of 2009 and 2017, there existed the bare minimum of financial and criminal laws, however there was no specific governing legislation for digital assets. During those years, most digital currency businesses thrived in what has been called a grey area of regulation, as the government did not acknowledge cryptocurrencies as a legitimate tender. The Bank of England, HM Treasury, and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) began collaborating in 2018 to formulate a regulatory policy in regard to cryptoassets, which resulted in the creation of the Cryptoassets Task Force.
In 2019, the FCA published guidelines on the classification of cryptoassets, identifying unmanned tokens, e-money tokens, and security tokens.
As of January 2020, the FCA took on the responsibility of Supervisor for the Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Counter-Terrorist Financing (CTF) programs.  Another notable development occurred three years later with the implementation of the Financial Services and Markets Act (FMSA).  This expanded the scope of regulation over cryptoassets, especially in relation to fiat-backed stablecoins and their payments systems. Also in 2023, the FCA published the Cryptoasset Financial Promotions Regime, which set out the first non-discriminatory rules for the sale of cryptoassets to residents of the UK, providing full protection for the customers regardless of the company's domicile.
In November 2024, the FCA and the Bank of England published joint reports outlining their intentions to bring cryptoassets within the regulatory perimeter in their entirety by 2026, demonstrating a consolidated approach. This was also the year that the Travel Rule was implemented in the UK.
During this period, the UK Gambling Commission (UKGC) also began to actively enforce existing laws against companies that used cryptocurrencies for payments. While the UKGC did not name cryptoassets, their position was that the 2005 Gambling Act continues to apply to all activities of licensed operators.
REGULATORY BODIES
In the United Kingdom, no single organization oversees the entire cryptocurrency ecosystem. Different agencies of primary importance are involved in the supervision of cryptocurrencies within the UK. These agencies have distinct responsibilities focusing on different aspects of cryptocurrency activities. These include the Bank of England, UK Gambling Commission, Advertising Standards Authority, HM Treasury, and the Financial Conduct Authority.
Financial Conduct Authority (FCA)
The FCA supervises cryptoasset firms doing business in or servicing UK consumers. Since January 2020, the FCA has acted as the designated supervisor of these firms. The FCA enforces UK advertising standards, consumer protection legislation, Brexit Advertising Standards as well as maintaining the public registry of cryptoasset companies operating in the UK crypto ecosystem
HM Treasury
The financial policies of HM Treasury include the cryptoasset's strategy. The HM treasury is responsible for the overall directions of the policies. It formulates and coordinates policy documents, and sets the strategies from within the UK and from other countries.
Co-founding the UK Cryptoassets Task Force in 2018 with the FCA and Bank of England was HM Treasury’s way of recognizing the growing importance of the cryptocurrency economy. Since then, it has published several consultation papers to expand and define the regulatory scope for digital assets.
Bank of England
Most cryptocurrency activity is not within the scope of the Bank of England’s direct oversight. From the perspective of digital assets, stablecoins, cryptocurrency, and the majority of the digital economy, the Bank of England is most concerned with financial system-wide risks. It examines what the regulatory and wider implications could be for cryptoassets on the UK's monetary and financial landscape.
The UK Gambling Commission (UKGC)
The UK Gambling Commission (UKGC) supervises gambling activities within the jurisdiction of the United Kingdom. It also regulates gaming establishments that pay their clients through cryptocurrency. The UKGC regards cryptocurrency the same as traditional currency for gambling service purposes. Gambling operators that work with cryptocurrencies as a payment option are required to follow the same compliance guidelines as all other operators within the United Kingdom.
Advertising Standards Authority (ASA)
The United Kingdom has set up authorities to regulate advert content, and the Advertising Standards Authority is the body that covers digital adverts. After the withdrawal of the temporary measures on cryptocurrency advertising in 2023, the ASA partnered with the FCA.
ASA has also claimed to work with the FCA and other government bodies in the UK to ensure compliance with the law through monitoring contravention of the ‘fair’ principle in advertising. It has launched a number of enforcement actions for deceptive advertising and lax advertising scrutiny for cryptocurrencies and related financial products. Violation of advertising regulations include advertising without risk disclosures, advertising without sufficient warning, as well as other forms of manipulation.
These authorities work together to ensure that consumers are protected, the integrity and reputation of the market is preserved, financial crime is minimized, and competition and innovation within the crypto markets of the UK is encouraged.
CURRENT REGULATORY FRAMEWORK
There is no single piece of legislation in the UK which aims to govern the use of cryptocurrency by its citizens. It is a patchwork of financial regulations, anti-money laundering rules, and sector-specific regulations created to deal with the challenges of emerging digital assets. The legal texts guiding cryptocurrency use in the UK include, the financial services and Markets Act 2023, the Travel Rule Implementation, the Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 and the Cryptoasset Promotions Regime.
AML/CTF Regulations
The regulations on money laundering, terrorist financing and crypto provide a framework for digital currency activity. Cryptocurrency exchange operators must obtain a registration with the financial and UK gambling authorities and comply with strict licensing conditions.
All registered and licensed exchange operators are obliged to comply with strict anti-money laundering and counter terrorist financing regulations. These rules include monitoring account activity and customer due diligence reporting of suspicious activity to the relevant authorities.
The UK Gambling Commission (UKGC)'s advanced Know Your Customer (KYC) and AML guidelines requiring real-time crediting and fund origin confirmation for wagers placed with crypto, also affect operators of crypto gambling.
Financial Promotions
The Financial Services and Markets Act of 2023 has permitted the control of promotions that involve cryptocurrency. The Act also states that firms dealing with cryptocurrency products or services targeting UK consumers should ensure that their communications are not vague, false or misleading in any form. For the purpose of avoiding scam advertisements, crypto promotions should be vetted and approved by the FCA prior to release. Advertisements should disclose risks and issues that accompany the products while providing appropriate information to the consumers. Entities dealing with cryptocurrency products are also required to ensure appropriate information is collected regarding the intended use of the products. This rule applies to foreign or overseas entities that deal with UK consumers.
Travel Rule
The UK is among many countries in the world that have implemented the Travel rule in their regulation of crypto asset service providers. This rule was made a global standard by the Financial Action Task Force. It requires crypto companies to obtain information that contains the origins and beneficiaries of the crypto and provide them to the relevant crypto asset service providers.
Taxation
HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) treat cryptoassets as property rather than currency. It also published guidance on capital gains tax and income tax obligations. HMRC applies current tax laws to transactions involving cryptoassets.  Depending on the specifics of their operations, people and companies may be subject to the Capital Gains Tax (CGT), Income Tax, Corporation Tax, and Value Added Tax (VAT).
When you dispose of cryptoassets, you are liable to capital gains tax. Events involving taxable disposal include: trading cryptocurrency for fiat money, trading one cryptocurrency for another, using cryptocurrency to buy products or services, and  giving cryptocurrency as a gift (apart from to a spouse or civil partner)
HMRC treats transactions in which people receive cryptoassets as a reward or payment as taxable income. The following situations may result in the application of income tax and national insurance contributions (NICs): getting paid in cryptocurrency for products or services (for example, as a freelancer), obtaining yield or staking rewards from decentralised finance (DeFi), mining or verifying transactions on a proof-of-stake or proof-of-work network (when done for profit), and obtaining cryptocurrency via incentive programs or airdrops (where a service has been rendered)
Exchanges, payment services, gambling operators, and investment firms are among the businesses involved in cryptoasset-related activities that are typically required to pay corporation tax on profits made from: Trading cryptoassets, Offering services based on cryptocurrency, Taking cryptocurrency payments, Commercial-scale mining or staking
Winnings from gambling, including those made with cryptoassets, are typically exempt from income tax and capital gains tax in the UK. This is due to the fact that gambling is not considered a taxable activity for private citizens. This holds true for the majority of conventional types of gambling, including lotteries, online casinos, and betting.
Gambling companies are not exempt, though, as they are required to pay Corporation Tax on their earnings from cryptocurrency gambling.
In accordance with the 2014 European Court of Justice decision in Hedqvist v. Skatteverket, HMRC has made it clear that trading cryptocurrencies for fiat money or other tokens is not subject to VAT. This implies that no VAT is owed when a person purchases or sells cryptoassets for personal use.
However, in the following situations, VAT might be applicable:
As with any other payment method, businesses that offer goods or services in exchange for cryptocurrency are required to account for VAT. If the services are in the VATable category, fees levied by cryptocurrency brokers or exchanges may be liable to VAT.
Penalties, interest, and investigations may follow nonreporting of taxable cryptocurrency transactions. If a taxpayer has underreported in the past, HMRC encourages them to voluntarily disclose it and, if needed, seek professional advice.
Gambling Regulations
The UKGC has created a regulatory framework to address the unique risks posed by cryptoassets in gambling operations as a result of the increasing use of cryptocurrency in gambling.
Standards for Licensing and Compliance
Every gambling establishment that takes cryptocurrency must have a current UKGC licence and adhere to the same strict guidelines as those that apply to traditional currency operators. This includes duties to promote responsible gaming and stop financial crime under the Gambling Act of 2005 and the Proceeds of Crime Act of 2002.
Improved KYC and AML Procedures
Operators are required by the UKGC to conduct enhanced KYC and AML checks on cryptocurrency transactions. This entails confirming each player's cryptocurrency and money source, going beyond simple identity verification; keeping an eye on all withdrawals and payments in real time to spot questionable activity; and exercising extra caution when transactions surpass predetermined thresholds (e.g., 2000 pounds).
Fairness and Openness of the Game
Proof that all games, whether proprietary or third-party, are audited and provably fair by design is required by the UKGC for gambling sites that accept cryptocurrency. This audit guarantees the presence of electronically verifiable randomness and fairness mechanisms.
Regulations for Payment and Wallets
Unless they are formally registered and regulated, operators of digital wallets must make sure they are run under non-custodial arrangements. Strict controls apply to direct cryptocurrency deposits and withdrawals, and in order to reduce volatility risk, player accounts frequently need to be converted to fiat money.
FUTURE DEVELOPMENTS
In order to handle the industry's explosive growth and new threats, the UK is aggressively moving forward with a major revision of its cryptocurrency regulations. By broadening the scope and enhancing the clarity of regulation across all crypto activities, these reforms seek to improve market integrity, protect consumers, and encourage innovation. Over the next few years, the UK's position as a global leader in the cryptocurrency ecosystem will be shaped by a number of impending legislative initiatives, consultations, and technological investigations.
Property (Digital Assets) Bill
A significant step was taken in 2025 when the Property (Digital Assets) Bill formally recognised cryptoassets and other digital assets as legal property in England and Wales. By defining ownership rights and dispute resolution procedures, this designation improves legal protections for businesses and consumers against fraud and scams involving digital assets.
Expansion of Regulated Crypto Activities
The UK government intends to gradually expand regulation to include a wide range of cryptocurrency services, building on the Property Bill and continuing consultations. They plan to regulate:
Cryptoasset issuance and redemption, including stablecoins
Services and exchanges for cryptocurrency payments
Trading, risk management, and investment
Activities related to lending, borrowing, and leverage (establishing a world-first framework for crypto lending)
Administration, custody, and protection of cryptoassets
Cryptoasset governance, staking, and validation
With clear responsibilities for businesses and safeguards against fraud, manipulation, and operational risks, this phased regulatory regime is expected to fully implement by 2026.
The FCA also announced a roadmap regarding the future of crypto policy, which shows an overview of likely considerations in years to come. This includes considerations of policies to prevent market abuses like insider trading and rules on intermediation, lending, and staking.
The regulatory developments surrounding cryptocurrencies in the UK have generated a variety of reactions from investors, industry players, legislators, and the general public. These reactions range from cautious optimism to serious concerns regarding the pace and direction of regulation.
The rapidly changing regulatory environment has presented operational challenges for many cryptocurrency businesses, especially startups and smaller companies that are juggling intricate AML, licensing, and financial promotion requirements.
In order to proactively meet expectations, industry associations and service providers are making investments in legal advisory services, compliance technologies, and cooperative projects with regulators.
